- Example: pumice has high porosity (many pores) but low permeability (pores are isolated bubbles); OR clay/shale has variable porosity but very low permeability because tiny pore spaces impede fluid flow (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the grain size, shape and sorting of sediment deposited in a wind-blown dune environment with sediment deposited as a scree at the base of a cliff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three properties compared contrastively for both environments: grain size (dune = fine to medium sand; scree = coarse, angular fragments varying in size); grain shape (dune = well-rounded, frosted; scree = angular, sharp edges); sorting (dune = well-sorted by wind winnowing; scree = poorly sorted, wide range of sizes). Stated as comparisons.
Secure: Two properties compared correctly for both environments.
Developing: One property compared correctly; or both environments described separately.
Emerging: One environment described with a grain property; other not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of grain size, shape and sorting as evidence for reconstructing the environment in which an ancient sedimentary rock was deposited.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three distinct lines of evidence evaluated with specific examples: (1) grain size indicates energy level (coarse = high energy rivers or beaches; fine = quiet deep water or lakes); (2) grain shape indicates transport distance and medium (rounded frosted = aeolian; rounded non-frosted = water; angular = scree/glacial); (3) sorting indicates energy consistency (well-sorted = beach or dune; poorly sorted = glacial or debris flow). Evaluative points about limitations (e.g. diagenesis/cementation can modify original porosity; multiple environments can produce similar grain sizes so one property alone is insufficient; well-rounded grains may be recycled not primary; colour from later oxidation may confuse interpretation).
Secure: Two lines of evidence with specific environments; some evaluation.
Developing: One line of evidence with partial environment link; limited evaluation.
Emerging: General statements about grain size with no specific environments or critical evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which layer of the Earth forms the foundation on which the tectonic plates float?
A) Inner core
B) Outer core
C) Asthenosphere
D) Continental crust
practice_questions.marks: C) Asthenosphere [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the scientist who proposed the hypothesis of sea-floor spreading in the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Harry Hess [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe three features of magnetic stripe patterns on the ocean floor that support sea-floor spreading.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each (up to 3):
• The stripes are symmetrical / mirror images on either side of the mid-ocean ridge [1]
• The stripes run parallel to the ridge [1]
• The stripes alternate between normal and reversed magnetic polarity [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why Alfred Wegener’s hypothesis of continental drift was not accepted by the scientific community in the early twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• He could not provide a credible mechanism to explain how continents move [1]
• No force was known to be capable of moving entire continents through solid ocean floor [1]
• Despite good observational evidence (jigsaw fit, fossils, matching formations), the absence of a mechanism meant the hypothesis was scientifically unconvincing / not testable [1]

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of oceanic crust and continental crust. In your answer, refer to thickness and composition.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per comparison, 1 for naming, 1 for giving both sides):
• Oceanic crust is 5–10 km thick; continental crust is 25–70 km thick [2]
• Oceanic crust is composed mainly of basalt (dense); continental crust is composed mainly of granite (less dense) [2]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the contribution of different scientists and methods to the development of plate tectonic theory. Consider the evidence they provided and reach a conclusion about which contribution was most significant.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers Wegener (jigsaw fit, fossils, formations — observational but lacking mechanism), Hess (sea-floor spreading — provided mechanism), Vine-Matthews-Morley (magnetic stripes — quantitative confirmation), GPS (modern direct measurement). Evaluates which was most significant with a justified reason (e.g. magnetic stripes because they provided a testable, quantitative record). Reaches a balanced conclusion.
Secure: Covers at least three contributions correctly; identifies the weakness in Wegener (no mechanism); some evaluation of significance.
Developing: Covers two contributions; limited comparison; conclusion present but brief.
Emerging: One contribution described; little or no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following rock types would make the best host for a hazardous waste disposal facility?
A) Permeable sandstone
B) Fractured limestone
C) Massive unfractured mudstone
D) Chalk with well-developed joint networks
practice_questions.marks: C) Massive unfractured mudstone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the synthetic liner placed beneath a landfill site to prevent leachate escaping into the ground.
practice_questions.marks: Geomembrane [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the water table is and explain how it relates to the formation of natural springs.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturated rock in an aquifer, below which all pore spaces are filled with water. (1)
- Where the water table intersects the ground surface — for example, on a hillside or in a valley — groundwater discharges naturally as a spring. (1)

practice_questions.text: A monitoring borehole records a groundwater nitrate concentration of 12 mg/L in January. By August, the concentration has risen to 48 mg/L. Calculate the percentage increase in nitrate concentration. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage increase = ((48 - 12) / 12) × 100 = (36 / 12) × 100 = 300%
[2 marks: 1 for correct method, 1 for correct answer]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a porous and permeable sandstone is a poor choice for the geological disposal of hazardous waste.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- Sandstone has high porosity, meaning it contains large pore spaces that the waste or its dissolved components would occupy. (1)
- Its high permeability means groundwater flows readily through it; any waste or leachate would be transported rapidly away from the disposal site by moving groundwater. (1)
- Contamination would spread widely into the groundwater system, potentially reaching wells and springs that supply drinking water far from the disposal site before detection. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological factors that determine whether a site is suitable for a domestic landfill. In your answer, consider both the rock type and the position relative to aquifers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses rock permeability, aquifer vulnerability, confining layers, water table depth and monitoring; recognises the multi-factor nature of siting decisions; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: At least three geological factors discussed with explanations; conclusion present.
Developing: Identifies relevant factors but explanation is limited; conclusion may be absent.
Emerging: Names one or two factors without explanation.

Key factors:
- Underlying rock must have low permeability to reduce leachate migration risk; clay or dense mudstone beneath the site provides a natural barrier even before engineered liners are added.
- The site should not overlie a major unconfined aquifer; the Chalk in south-east England, for example, has highly developed fracture networks that transmit contaminants rapidly, making it a high-risk host.
- A confining layer (impermeable stratum) between the landfill base and any aquifer below adds natural protection; the greater the thickness and continuity of this layer, the safer the site.
- The water table must be deep enough below the base of the waste to provide a buffer zone; a site where the water table is within a few metres of the surface is high risk.
- The regional groundwater flow direction matters: monitoring boreholes should be placed downgradient; any breach will move in that direction.
- Proximity to Source Protection Zones (inner zones around public water supply boreholes) should disqualify a site.

Conclusion: No single geological factor is decisive; siting decisions require combining rock permeability, aquifer classification, water table depth and groundwater flow direction into a holistic assessment. The most important principle is to maximise the natural geological barrier between the waste and any usable groundwater, and to supplement this with engineered barriers and long-term monitoring. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which sedimentary rock forms from the evaporation of seawater in hot, arid conditions and contains the mineral halite?
A) Limestone
B) Shale
C) Evaporite
D) Sandstone
practice_questions.marks: C) Evaporite [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the sedimentary structure formed when an underwater avalanche of sediment produces a bed with coarse grains at the base fining upward to silt at the top.
practice_questions.marks: Graded bedding [1 mark] (accept turbidite deposit)

practice_questions.text: Describe how the properties of breccia and conglomerate differ and explain what each tells you about the transport history of the sediment.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- Breccia has angular coarse clasts, indicating short transport distance (close to source, little abrasion)
- Conglomerate has rounded coarse clasts, indicating long transport distance (abrasion during prolonged transport by river or high-energy waves)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how cross-bedding in a desert sandstone provides evidence for the direction of wind transport at the time of deposition.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for:
- Cross-bedding consists of inclined laminae (foresets) within the main horizontal beds (1 mark)
- The laminae dip in the direction of the prevailing current / wind at the time of deposition (1 mark)
- Large-scale curved cross-beds in a desert sandstone (well-sorted, well-rounded frosted grains) indicate migration of aeolian dunes, so the dip direction of the foresets gives the palaeowind direction (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sequence of rocks from base to top shows: conglomerate → sandstone → shale → limestone with coral fossils. Interpret the changing environment of deposition as you move upward through the sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear sequence of four environments linked to the rocks: conglomerate at base = high-energy coarse deposition (braided river or beach, long transport); sandstone = moderate energy, shallower marine or fluvial; shale = quiet, low-energy water (deep water or lagoon); limestone with coral = shallow, warm, well-oxygenated marine environment. Each rock linked to its environment with evidence.
Secure: Three rocks correctly interpreted with environment; one missing or partially correct.
Developing: Two rocks correctly interpreted; sequence direction followed but environments partially wrong.
Emerging: One rock identified with an environment; sequence not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well sedimentary structures can be used as evidence for interpreting the environment of deposition of an ancient rock sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three sedimentary structures discussed with their environmental evidence and limitations: (1) cross-bedding indicates current direction and dune migration in fluvial or aeolian settings, but cross-beds can form in both rivers and deserts so additional evidence (grain shape, redness) is needed; (2) graded bedding is a strong indicator of turbidite/deep-sea origin because the mechanism (density settling from a turbidity current) is specific, though some graded beds form in other settings; (3) desiccation cracks confirm periodic subaerial exposure (tidal flat, desert lake margin) but must be distinguished from later shrinkage cracks. Evaluative conclusion: structures are powerful but work best in combination with grain size, fossils and rock type.
Secure: Two structures with specific environments and one evaluative point.
Developing: One structure with environment; limited evaluation.
Emerging: General statements about sedimentary rocks with no specific structures or environments.

practice_questions.text:
At which plate boundary type is new oceanic crust created?
A) Conservative
B) Convergent (subduction)
C) Continent–continent collision
D) Divergent
practice_questions.marks: D) Divergent [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the zone of deep earthquakes that follows the path of a subducting plate into the mantle.
practice_questions.marks: Benioff zone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between the geological activity at a divergent plate boundary and a conservative plate boundary.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per comparison, 1 for naming, 1 for giving both sides):
• Divergent: volcanic activity occurs (basaltic magma erupts at ridges); conservative: little or no volcanic activity [2]
• Divergent: new oceanic crust is created; conservative: no crust is created or destroyed [2]
Accept: divergent produces rift valleys / ridges; conservative produces large strike-slip faults [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how andesitic magma is produced above a subduction zone.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The subducting oceanic plate warms and releases water/volatiles as it descends [1]
• These fluids rise into the overlying mantle wedge, lowering its melting point and causing partial melting [1]
• The resulting magma is enriched in silica compared to basalt, producing andesitic magma [1]

practice_questions.text: A mid-ocean ridge is spreading at a half-rate of 3.5 cm per year. Calculate how far apart two points on opposite plates will be after 2 million years. Express your answer in kilometres. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Full spreading rate = 2 × 3.5 = 7 cm/year. Distance = 7 cm/yr × 2,000,000 yr = 14,000,000 cm = 140 km [2 marks: 1 for doubling the half-rate, 1 for correct final answer with units]. Accept: 140 km.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological evidence that would allow a geologist to distinguish between an ocean–continent convergent boundary and a continent–continent collision zone. Consider the structures, magmas, and topographic features produced at each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Compares structures (trench + island arc vs mountain belt without trench), magma types (andesitic, explosive at subduction; granitic, intrusive at collision), topography (deep trench vs high plateau/mountain range), seismicity (Benioff zone deep earthquakes at subduction; shallower earthquakes at collision); gives real examples (Andes/Nazca vs Himalaya/Indo-Australian); evaluates which features are most diagnostic; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly identifies at least three distinguishing features across the two boundary types with examples; some evaluation.
Developing: Identifies one or two differences; limited evidence; little evaluation.
Emerging: Partial understanding of one boundary type; no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following rock types would provide the best foundation for a large dam?
A) Highly weathered clay-rich shale
B) Soluble evaporite (halite)
C) Massive unfractured granite
D) Loosely cemented sandstone with open joints
practice_questions.marks: C) Massive unfractured granite [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the UK national organisation that provides geological maps and borehole records for civil engineering projects.
practice_questions.marks: British Geological Survey (BGS) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two geological features that must be assessed before constructing a dam.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for any two of:
- The strength and permeability of the foundation rock, to ensure it can support the structure and will not allow reservoir water to seep through. (1)
- The dip direction of strata, to check that bedding planes do not create seepage pathways beneath or around the dam. (1)
- The presence and orientation of faults and joints, which can reduce rock mass strength and create permeability pathways. (1)

practice_questions.text: A motorway cutting exposes strata dipping at 25° toward the road. The safe angle for this rock type is 15°. By how many degrees does the actual dip exceed the safe angle? State one consequence of this for slope stability.
practice_questions.marks:
Excess dip = 25 − 15 = 10°
[1 mark for correct calculation]
Consequence: rock blocks may slide along the dipping bedding planes toward the road, causing a planar landslide. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Channel Tunnel was bored through the Chalk Marl rather than through the overlying Chalk.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- The Chalk Marl is a clay-rich layer within the Chalk sequence that has very low permeability, meaning minimal groundwater would flow into the tunnel during and after construction. (1)
- The Chalk Marl has adequate compressive strength for tunnelling — it can stand for a reasonable period without support after excavation, unlike highly fractured or very soft rocks. (1)
- The overlying Chalk has a well-developed fracture and joint network that makes it highly permeable; boring through it would have caused severe groundwater inflow, making tunnelling extremely difficult and costly. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological factors that make one river valley more suitable than another for building a large dam and reservoir. Use geological evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates multiple geological factors (rock type, dip, faults/joints, permeability) with clear explanation of how each affects dam safety; compares favourable and unfavourable conditions; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: At least three geological factors explained with both favourable and unfavourable conditions identified; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes relevant factors but lacks comparison or full explanation of mechanisms.
Emerging: Names one or two factors with limited explanation.

Favourable conditions:
- Valley cut into competent, massive igneous or metamorphic rock (e.g. granite) with no faults: provides strong, impermeable dam foundation and valley walls that will not settle or seep.
- Strata dipping upstream, into the reservoir: water entering the bedding planes travels down-dip away from the dam, so seepage under the dam is reduced.
- Absence of soluble rock types (evaporites, karstified limestone): prevents underground dissolution channels forming that would allow reservoir leakage.
- Low regional permeability: entire valley floor and sides act as a natural seal, retaining reservoir water.

Unfavourable conditions:
- Fault crossing the dam axis: fault zones are weaker and often more permeable; differential movement under reservoir loading can damage the structure (e.g. St Francis Dam failure, 1928).
- Strata dipping downstream: water travels down the bedding planes from the reservoir, passes under the dam and emerges beyond it, and the same planes can act as slip surfaces.
- Karst limestone: dissolution channels and caves allow direct loss of reservoir water with no natural filtration.
- Shallow depth to groundwater: complicates construction and may cause reservoir leakage into adjacent lowlands.

Conclusion: The most important single factor is the integrity and impermeability of the foundation and valley-side rock. A granite valley with upstream-dipping strata and no faults represents ideal conditions; a valley in faulted limestone with downstream-dipping beds represents serious challenges that may require extensive grouting or may render the site unfeasible. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which metamorphic rock is produced from limestone by either contact or regional metamorphism and is non-foliated?
A) Slate
B) Schist
C) Metaquartzite
D) Marble
practice_questions.marks: D) Marble [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the zone of thermally altered rock that surrounds an igneous intrusion due to contact metamorphism.
practice_questions.marks: Metamorphic aureole [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between slate and schist.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for two of the following:
- Slate has microscopic mica grains (invisible to naked eye); schist has visible, larger mica crystals
- Slate shows slaty cleavage (fine-scale); schist shows schistosity (coarser foliation with visible mica alignment)
- Slate forms by low-grade regional metamorphism; schist forms by medium-to-high-grade regional metamorphism
- Schist may contain porphyroblasts such as garnet; slate does not
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why metamorphism is described as a solid-state process, and why this distinguishes it from igneous processes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for:
- In metamorphism, rocks are transformed by heat and/or pressure but do not melt (remain solid throughout) (1 mark)
- Minerals recrystallise in the solid state to form new, stable minerals suited to the new temperature and pressure conditions (1 mark)
- In igneous processes, rock melts to form magma before crystallising; if melting occurs during what appears to be metamorphism, the product is igneous, not metamorphic (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare contact metamorphism and regional metamorphism, referring to the scale of the process, the agents involved and the type of rock produced.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear comparison on three criteria (scale: contact = localised around intrusion; regional = large area of crust during orogeny); agents (contact = mainly heat from intrusion, low directed pressure; regional = heat AND directed pressure from burial and mountain-building); products (contact = typically non-foliated rocks; regional = foliated rocks such as slate and schist). All stated as direct comparisons.
Secure: Two criteria compared correctly for both types.
Developing: One criterion compared; or both types described separately without direct comparison.
Emerging: One type described with limited reference to the other.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how the texture of a metamorphic rock provides evidence for the conditions under which it formed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three distinct texture features discussed as evidence for conditions: (1) slaty cleavage in slate indicates low-grade regional metamorphism with directed pressure aligning microscopic mica perpendicular to stress, at relatively low temperature and pressure; (2) schistosity in schist indicates higher-grade regional metamorphism with sufficient temperature for large mica crystals to grow and align; visible garnet porphyroblasts confirm higher temperature; (3) non-foliated interlocking texture in marble/metaquartzite indicates either contact metamorphism (heat but little directed pressure) or minerals lacking platy habit (calcite/quartz). Evaluative point: texture alone may not distinguish contact from low-grade regional metamorphism without context; field setting (aureole vs regional belt) is also needed.
Secure: Two texture features with conditions and one evaluative point.
Developing: One texture feature with partial conditions; limited evaluation.
Emerging: General statements about metamorphism with no specific textures or conditions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what a rose diagram shows?
A) The thickness of rock units in a borehole plotted to vertical scale
B) The frequency of measurements in different compass directions, shown as petals on a circular diagram
C) The relationship between grain size and depth in a sedimentary sequence
D) A vertical slice through the geology along a line drawn on a map
practice_questions.marks: B) The frequency of measurements in different compass directions, shown as petals on a circular diagram [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the combined field instrument used to measure both the strike and the dip of a rock surface.
practice_questions.marks: Compass clinometer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a simplified geological map shows and state one way it differs from a professional BGS geological map.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- A simplified geological map shows the surface distribution of rock units, their boundaries, faults and fold axes in a small exam-format area. (1)
- It uses fewer rock units and removes minor detail compared with the full-scale BGS 1:50,000 maps, making it manageable for exam use. (Accept other valid differences, e.g. scale, level of detail, number of units.) (1)

practice_questions.text: A geological map shows a rock boundary forming a V-shape that points downstream (in the direction water flows). What does this tell you about the dip direction of the strata? Explain your reasoning using the rule of Vs.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- The rule of Vs states that a boundary crossing a valley produces a V-shape pointing in the dip direction when beds are inclined, or pointing upstream for horizontal or gently downstream-dipping beds. (1)
- A V pointing downstream shows that the strata dip downstream, in the same direction as the stream flows. (1)
- The beds must dip downstream more steeply than the valley floor; a gentler downstream dip would still give a V pointing upstream. (1)

practice_questions.text: A geological map shows the following sequence from bottom to top: mudstone, limestone (cut by a fault), sandstone unconformably overlying the limestone. Sequence these geological events from oldest to youngest, giving the evidence for each step.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correctly evidenced step (up to 4):
1. Deposition of mudstone — oldest because it lies below all other units (superposition). (1)
2. Deposition of limestone above the mudstone — younger than the mudstone by superposition. (1)
3. Faulting of the limestone — the fault cuts the limestone so must post-date its deposition (cross-cutting relationships). (1)
4. Erosion followed by deposition of sandstone unconformably above the limestone — the unconformity represents a gap in the record; the sandstone is the youngest unit because it overlies all others (superposition). (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of fieldwork skills for understanding and interpreting a geological map in an examination context. Refer to specific skills and techniques in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly links specific fieldwork skills (compass clinometer, graphic logs, field sketches, rose diagrams) to map interpretation tasks; evaluates both the benefits and the limitations; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Discusses at least three specific skills with explanation of how they aid map interpretation; conclusion present.
Developing: Lists relevant skills but explanation of the link to map interpretation is limited; conclusion may be absent.
Emerging: Brief descriptive account of one or two skills without evaluative comment.

Key links between fieldwork and map interpretation:
- Compass clinometer use in the field teaches the student what dip angles feel like and how they translate to map patterns; students who have measured a 30° dip can visualise how that would appear as a V-pattern on a map.
- Graphic log construction in the field trains students to read vertical sequences; this directly prepares them for interpreting borehole logs and stratigraphic columns on the exam paper.
- Field sketching and annotated drawings develop the skill of extracting and labelling geological features — essential for annotating map extracts and cross-sections under exam conditions.
- Rose diagrams constructed from field joint measurements train students to recognise dominant structural trends; in the exam, rose diagrams appear as data to interpret rather than construct, but familiarity with the data type is necessary.
- Practising the geological code of conduct and safe working develops professional geological thinking that informs field-question answers about survey design.

Limitations:
- Fieldwork is centre-specific; the location, rock types and structures will differ from those on the exam map, so transferable skills matter more than site-specific knowledge.
- Time constraints mean that not every map skill can be directly practised in the field; some must also be practised through paper exercises.

Conclusion: Fieldwork is valuable because it develops the observational habits and spatial reasoning that underlie all map interpretation skills. However, its greatest contribution is building intuition about real geological structures rather than directly rehearsing exam tasks. Students who combine fieldwork experience with systematic map-reading practice are best prepared. [6 marks]
